what_it_does: A brain-controlled prosthetic arm works by reading electrical signals from the brain through electrodes placed on the scalp (called EEG — electroencephalography), then classifying those signals in real time to decide which movement the person intends to make. The challenge is that this entire pipeline — filtering the raw signal, extracting features, running a neural-network classifier — must happen in milliseconds on a small, low-power chip embedded in the prosthetic device. This paper presents CognitiveArm, a system that automates the search for a neural-network design that is both accurate and small enough to fit on embedded hardware, using an evolutionary search (inspired by natural selection) to explore many design choices simultaneously and find a good balance between accuracy and resource cost. The final model is compressed further by removing unimportant connections (pruning) and representing weights with fewer bits (using smaller numbers than the default), so it runs efficiently on the target hardware. A voice-command mode allows the user to switch control modes without needing a separate physical button. Details on the specific hardware target, latency figures, and accuracy comparisons are from the abstract and may not be fully representative.
